newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares plagued by political uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares plagued by political uncertainty.

text.p: Turkish shares have plummeted 15 percent this week in persistent doubts about the government's ability to weather a row with the military and to push ahead with badly-needed economic reforms, brokers said on Wednesday.
The IMKB National-100 index fell 4.92 percent, or 71 points, to close at 1,372 in a downtrend which earlier this week had already knocked 10.48 percent of shares from Friday's close of 1,612.

Nervous sentiment depressed trading volume, which dropped to 15.20 trillion lira ($122.5 million) from 28.73 trillion on Tuesday as investors shrunk away from a market plagued by fears of political instability.

"Amid this instability it is difficult for the stock market to be positive. Investors are using the opportunity for selling and until the political tension is resolved this is the way the market will continue," said Tuncay Tursucu of General Finans.
Brokers said attention was focused on Thursday's cabinet meeting, which was expected to throw some light on the political outlook.

Bond yields were driven higher for the third consecutive day, jumping 6-8 percentage points to around 110 percent. A fall in the lira to 124,190 against the dollar prompted fresh central bank intervention and the Turkish currency ended the day at 124,070, down from a close of 123,710 on Tuesday.

A weekend warning from the military that the Islamist-led government should rein in Moslem activism has undermined market confidence in the coalition's ability to concentrate on fulfilling bold privatisation promises.

Official forecasts of $5 billion revenues from sell-offs in 1997 had been the engine behind a 65 percent leap in share prices this year, before Friday's statement from the National Security Council, dominated by the powerful military.
"One of the reasons for the negative influence on the market is that nothing definite has come out of the privatisation efforts," said Meksa Securities broker Huseyn Istanbullu.

The sell-offs are a key aspect of bold revenue-raising packages announced by Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan since he came to power eight months ago with the aim of wiping out the burden on public finances of massive deficits.

Recent economic figures have dented market faith in the ability of his government to make good on its economic promises and tackle the fundamental structural problems of taxation and a costly social security system.

February wholesale prices rose 6.2 percent on the month and 78.6 percent for the year, the statistics office announced on Tuesday. Consumer prices were up a monthly 5.7 percent and 77.7 percent annually. Analysts had forecast a month-on-month rise of 4.5-5.5 percent.
Brokers said one of the main sources of anxiety was the reported refusal of Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, to approve the National Security Council statement.
"Erbakan's stance of not signing the NSC statement is exerting considerable pressure on the stock exchange," said Nafiz Mert, a broker at Baskent Securities.
However, the comment on Tuesday by conservative coalition partner Tansu Ciller that she would not abandon the alliance has given some comfort to the market.
Aside from the political worries, underlying sentiment in the market remained positive although any recovery was dependent on a positive signal from within the government, brokers said.
"If any positive news was to come out, however unlikely that is in the short-term, there could be a rise in the index to 1,600 points," Mert said.
